title: The EPA’s Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn’t Doing Its Job Anymore
gist: A Floodlight investigation finds the EPA's ASPECT chemical-detection plane has decayed: only seven emergency responses since early 2021, sensors that no longer deliver results in minutes (manual analysis takes about a week), missed toxics at the 2025 Smitty's Supply fire, and a no-bid $1.7M Telops sensor replacement that former program scientists say fixes the wrong problem amid rising chemical accidents.

insights.claim: The EPA's ASPECT chemical-detection plane flew almost 80 emergency missions in its first two decades (about four a year) but has averaged roughly one a year over the past five years, with just seven emergency responses since early 2021.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Federal airborne chemical-emergency monitoring capacity has eroded, shifting detection burden to local responders and private testers.
insights.locator: During its first two decades, the plane flew

insights.claim: The ASPECT plane did not respond to at least 80 chemical emergencies this year, including the October Toledo, Ohio glycidyl methacrylate tank leak that forced hundreds to evacuate and sent more than 50 to hospitals.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Gaps in federal monitoring raise liability and community-health exposure for chemical operators after incidents.

insights.claim: Accidental chemical releases are rising: the US Chemical Safety Board tracked 133 last year, up from 83 in 2021, even as the Trump administration proposes rolling back safeguards such as independent safety audits and community hazard disclosures.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Rising incident frequency plus deregulation increases tail risk for chemical, refining and industrial operators and their insurers.
insights.locator: The decline comes as accidental chemical releases

insights.claim: ASPECT's decline began when a 2019 EPA reorganization ordered staff to relocate to Texas or face termination, causing PhD-level program leads to leave, and the EPA failed to replace them with scientists experienced in airborne chemical detection.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Institutional knowledge loss, not hardware, can disable government technical programs; a pattern relevant to agency-capability risk.
insights.quote: They lost the institutional knowledge of the program, and quite frankly, lost the momentum of the program,
insights.locator: How the Program Lost Its Way

insights.claim: After the original ASPECT managers left, the program stopped proactively tracking emergencies and urging on-scene coordinators to deploy the plane, which now stays in a Texas hangar until requested.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Process changes, not capability, explain the drop in deployments.
insights.locator: Former ASPECT program managers say they used to actively track

insights.claim: In the 2023 Norfolk Southern East Palestine derailment, ASPECT was not requested until more than two days later, missed the vinyl chloride vent-and-burn, and collected only eight minutes of chemical data; the NTSB later concluded the vent-and-burn was unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Slow federal monitoring contributed to costly, possibly avoidable emergency decisions; the EPA inspector general is auditing the response.
insights.locator: A Missed Opportunity in East Palestine

insights.claim: At the August 2025 Smitty's Supply fire in Roseland, Louisiana, the EPA published ASPECT results showing pollutants far below harmful levels, but whistleblower Robert Kroutil's manual reanalysis of the raw data found high concentrations of toluene, trichloroethylene and naphthalene that could have endangered nearby communities.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Official all-clear air data can understate exposure, a factor in ongoing class-action litigation against Smitty's.
insights.locator: A later analysis of the raw flight data

insights.claim: In June the EPA inspector general found the ASPECT plane can no longer provide chemical data within five minutes as designed; manual analysis takes about a week, and the EPA failed to tell on-scene coordinators the program was not working as designed.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: A week's delay makes the data useless for evacuation decisions, undermining federal emergency-response credibility.
insights.locator: In June, the EPA inspector general confirmed

insights.claim: The EPA bypassed competitive bidding to award Canadian firm Telops, owned by Exosens, a $1.7 million contract for replacement ASPECT sensors, with integration not complete until early to mid 2027.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: A small no-bid federal contract win for Exosens/Telops in airborne gas-detection hyperspectral sensing.
insights.locator: EPA officials blamed the delays on old sensors

insights.claim: Five former ASPECT staff and independent infrared spectrometer expert Chris Manning argue the Telops sensors, mostly field-tested on methane leak tracking, are slower, less sensitive and less suited to moving targets than the old Bomem sensors, making them a poor replacement though a possible complement.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Methane-focused sensing tech may not generalize to complex industrial toxic plumes; procurement may degrade capability.
insights.quote: To say, ‘We're just going to replace these other two instruments’ … I mean, that’s ludicrous,
insights.locator: Chris Manning, an infrared spectrometer expert

insights.claim: ASPECT's old sensors' AI software was never retrained after an electrical malfunction despite a 2023 retraining plan from contract scientists, which former staff say is the real cause of the failures rather than worn-out hardware.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Neglected model maintenance, not sensor age, can break AI-dependent detection systems.
insights.locator: The old sensors had problems, too

insights.claim: Former ASPECT scientist Robert Kroutil predicts the program will keep deteriorating and the EPA will be flying blind unless major changes are made.
insights.speaker: Ames Alexander
insights.so_what: Expect continued gaps in federal chemical-emergency monitoring absent reform or oversight action.
insights.quote: Unless major changes are made at EPA and with the ASPECT program, it is not going to get any better and EPA will be flying blind.
insights.locator: In the affidavit submitted to the Government Accountability Project
